opus-5.5.text:
I think the jump from GPT-2 to GPT-4 is one of the most striking things we've seen in the history of AI, and it's worth being concrete about what changed. GPT-2, back in 2019, could produce text that was locally coherent. It could keep a paragraph going in a plausible style, but it would lose the thread fairly quickly. It couldn't reliably do arithmetic, it couldn't follow complex instructions, and you wouldn't trust it with anything resembling reasoning. GPT-4, just four years later, can pass professional exams, write and debug nontrivial code, work through multi-step problems, and act as a pretty capable general assistant across a huge range of domains.

What I find most useful is thinking about the inputs that produced that jump. At Epoch we spend a lot of time tracking these. The training compute between GPT-2 and GPT-4 went up by something like four orders of magnitude, so on the order of ten thousand times more compute. Part of that came from spending far more money on training runs. Part came from better hardware. And then there are algorithmic improvements, meaning better architectures, better data, and better training recipes. Our estimates suggest these effectively reduce the compute you need for a given level of performance by a factor of a few every year. If you put those together, the effective scale-up is enormous.

The interesting point is that much of this was fairly predictable in aggregate. Scaling laws told us loss would keep going down smoothly as we scaled. What's harder to predict is which specific capabilities emerge at which point, like when a model goes from being useless at coding to being genuinely helpful. So the aggregate trend is smooth, but the downstream qualitative experience can feel quite discontinuous.

I'd also say people tend to underrate how big that jump was, because it happened gradually in public view and we adapt quickly to new baselines. If you showed someone in 2019 what GPT-4 could do, I think most researchers would have been surprised it was achievable that soon. And that matters for forecasting. If the inputs keep growing at anything like the recent rate, and Epoch's work suggests there's room to keep scaling compute for several more years, then we should take seriously the possibility of another jump of similar magnitude, or larger, within the next several years.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-2 could produce locally coherent, plausible text but lost the thread and could not be trusted with reasoning, distinguishing fluent writing from substantive insight.

r002.rationale: It describes GPT-4 as a capable general assistant that can handle exams, code, and multi-step problems, marking a shift to practical usefulness.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to put some numbers on this, because the jump is really quite striking when you look at the inputs. GPT-2 was trained in 2019 with something on the order of ten to the twenty-one floating point operations. GPT-4, by our estimates, is somewhere around ten to the twenty-five. So that's roughly a ten-thousand-fold increase in training compute over about four years. And that's just compute. Over the same period you also had substantial algorithmic improvements, better data, larger and more carefully curated datasets, and then the whole layer of post-training, RLHF and so on, that didn't really exist in a meaningful form for GPT-2.

So when people look at the capability difference and say, well, GPT-2 could barely write a coherent paragraph and GPT-4 can pass the bar exam, that feels like a discontinuity. But I'd push back on the framing a bit. If you plot it against the inputs, it's actually what you'd expect from fairly smooth scaling. The reason it looks like a jump is that compute spending was growing at something like four or five x per year, which is just an extraordinarily fast pace by the standards of basically any other technology. So you get what looks like a qualitative leap because the quantity of effort going in was increasing exponentially, and the loss curves, the benchmark curves, were responding more or less as the scaling laws predicted.

Now, I'd add a caveat. The scaling laws tell you about loss, about next-token prediction. The mapping from loss to the capabilities people actually care about, reasoning, coding, passing exams, is much less well understood, and there are cases where capabilities appear to emerge somewhat abruptly on specific benchmarks even though the underlying loss is improving smoothly. Some of that is a measurement artifact, how you score the task, but I don't think all of it is. So I'd say the GPT-2 to GPT-4 jump is mostly explained by the inputs, and it's mostly predictable in hindsight, but it's a good reminder that the thing we're able to forecast well is the thing that's easy to measure, not necessarily the thing that matters.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a pretty dramatic jump. GPT-2 could produce text that was locally plausible, but it would often lose coherence over longer passages, and it wasn’t reliably useful for accomplishing tasks. With GPT-4, you have a system that can write code, explain difficult concepts, and follow fairly complicated instructions across a wide range of domains.

What’s striking is that this happened within a few years, largely by scaling up the same broad approach, alongside improvements in training and how these systems are made to follow instructions. That suggests we should take further improvements seriously.

But I’d distinguish performance on a particular task from the ability to do an entire job. GPT-4 still makes mistakes, and getting a system to reliably carry out extended projects is a different challenge from getting it to answer individual questions well. So the progress is substantial, while the implications for fully automating work are more uncertain.

r002.rationale: It contrasts GPT-2’s lack of reliable usefulness for tasks with GPT-4’s ability to perform practical tasks such as writing code and following complex instructions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very substantial jump. With GPT-2, you could see that the model had learned quite a lot about language, but it was difficult to get it to perform useful tasks reliably. By GPT-4, you have a system that can write code, explain complex ideas, and solve a fairly broad range of problems, often at a level that makes it useful in actual work.

What’s striking is that much of this progress came from scaling up broadly similar methods: more computation, more data, and larger models, alongside improvements in training. We didn’t need to discover an entirely new paradigm between GPT-2 and GPT-4 to get that increase in capabilities.

That makes me take further scaling quite seriously. It doesn’t establish that progress will continue at the same rate, or that these systems will become reliable in every domain. But it’s strong evidence that relatively general training methods can produce a much wider range of capabilities than you might have expected from looking at GPT-2 alone.
